title: Review findings, one lens
description: What one review lens writes to <target>/review-reports/<lens>.findings.json. Infrastructure/scripts/render_review_report.py validates it against this file, assigns each finding a stable ID, computes counts and overall risk, and renders the HTML; none of those are written by hand. Severity, confidence, evidence, and lens ownership are defined in Infrastructure/rules/review-contract.md.

lens.description: The lens prefix: CE code, MR methodology, DN numbers, CC consistency, AS provenance (AI skeptic).

target.description: The project shown in the report header: the target directory's name, or 'Research Project' when it has none.

review_date.description: The day of the review, YYYY-MM-DD. The renderer adds no timestamp of its own, so a re-render is byte-identical.

summary.description: Two to four sentences on what was found and why the overall risk is what it is.

context.description: Design context such as identification strategy, treatment, outcome, and clustering level. Mark each value '(provided)' or '(inferred)'; write 'Not specified' where it is unknown.

files_reviewed.description: Every file the lens read, as a path relative to the target.

findings.description: Findings and Questions for the author. A Question has severity QUESTION.

not_suggestion.description: SUGGESTION belongs to the code lens only.

check_id.description: The check family, from the lens's list below. It drives the stable ID and deduplication, so pick the owning family, not the nearest-sounding one.

severity.description: Impact if true (review-contract.md section 3). QUESTION marks a Question for the author, which has no severity.

confidence.description: high only when command output, documentation, or the quoted lines show the problem; low confidence is always a QUESTION.

line.description: First line of the quoted evidence.

explanation.description: Why it matters: the consequence for a result or claim.

fix.description: The concrete change that resolves it.

refutation.description: Required for HIGH and CRITICAL: what the reviewer checked to try to disprove the finding, and why it still stands.

related.description: Check families or finding IDs in other lenses that touch the same issue.

evidence.description: A finding with quoted evidence gives line and quote; a finding about something missing gives looked_in instead.

claim.description: What is wrong, in one sentence.

found.description: What the reviewer saw, in words.

quote.description: The exact code or text, copied, not paraphrased. The stable ID hashes it, so it survives line shifts.

verified_by.description: How it was checked: a command and its result, a documentation page, or 'the quoted lines'.

command.description: The command run, when there was one.

looked_in.description: For a missing step: where the reviewer looked, by file and section.

oneOf.description: Code that errors or cannot run as written.
Wrong logic: indexing, conditions, operators, overwritten objects.
Join or merge cardinality, unmatched keys, many-to-many.
Missing-value handling: na.rm, NA in filters and comparisons, missing as zero.
Type coercion: leading zeros lost, destring force, parsed types.
Randomness without a seed, or a seed set in the wrong place.
Absolute or machine-specific paths and other reproducibility breaks.
Efficiency or readability; SUGGESTION only.
Identification and research design: DiD, IV, RD, matching, event studies.
Standard errors, clustering, small numbers of clusters.
Regression specification: controls, functional form, logs with zeros.
Survey weights: missing, wrong unit (person vs. household), unrescaled pooled.
Dollar comparisons across time without a deflator; SA mixed with NSA.
Survey and sampling error: MOEs, overlapping periods, geography vintages.
Sample construction as a design choice: selection, attrition, unit of analysis.
Many outcomes tested within one claim family.
A number in the document differs from the output that produced it.
Arithmetic or transformation: differences, ratios, log points read as percent.
Rounding inconsistent with the source or with another mention.
A number that cannot be traced to any output.
Text and tables, or two tables, that disagree with each other.
The sample or universe the text describes differs from the code's.
A variable's definition in the text differs from its construction.
The method the text describes differs from the estimation.
Causal wording that the design does not support.
Interpretation and units: percent vs. percentage points, sign, direction.
A choice in the code (filter, recode, exclusion) the text does not disclose.
The data source, years, or vintage the text names differ from the code's.
A table or figure label, note, or caption that misdescribes its content.
A citation that does not exist, or a finding attributed to a real source that does not contain it.
An external figure (for example BLS or Census) that differs from its source.
A function, argument, or default that does not exist or does not behave as used.
A dataset variable or code that does not exist in the named source or vintage.
A comment or section header that says something the code does not do.
An edge-case test showing an operation that feeds a key result breaks.
